item.title: Tensor Network Simulation of Dynamic Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — DMRG-based tensor network simulation natively evaluates dynamic circuits via single-path stochastic sampling and multi-path branch ensemble tracking on MPS and TTN structures, achieving scalable branch propagation with bounded peak memory on 27-qubit random circuits.

Grade 0.389 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Innocenzo Fulginiti, Alessandro Poggiali, Christian Mendl

Figure

Runtime (left) and peak memory usage (right) versus qubit count for dynamic GHZ state preparation comparing unpruned multi-path simulation against single-path sampling with 16, 64, and 256 runs.

Asks

How can tensor-network DMRG algorithms be extended to classically simulate dynamic quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward without exponential path overhead?

But

Evaluated up to 27 qubits and depth 8; fixed bond dimensions χ∈{8,16,32}; multi-path branch count capped at M=8.

Tools

DMRG quantum circuit simulation · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) · Single-path stochastic sampling · Multi-path branch pruning

Abstract

Dynamic circuits, which incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations, extend the expressive power of quantum programs and are central to applications such as quantum error correction, state preparation, and distributed quantum algorithms. However, their classical simulation is challenging due to the exponential growth of execution branches induced by mid-circuit measurements. In this work, we develop a tensor network approach for simulating dynamic circuits by extending a DMRG-based method for quantum circuit simulation to support dynamic circuit operations. To address the exponential proliferation of execution branches, we introduce and compare two strategies: a single-path stochastic approach that samples individual measurement outcomes, and a multi-path approach that maintains an ensemble of branches. We benchmark these methods on standard dynamic circuits, including the teleportation protocol and GHZ state preparation, as well as on random dynamic circuits. Our analysis explores the trade-offs between simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. These results provide a practical and scalable framework for the classical simulation of dynamic circuits.

item.title: Lattice Lindbladian simulation by patching and merging
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulates generic lattice Lindbladian observables with gate count 𝒪((Nt)3/2−1/(4d+2)polylog(Nt/ε)) per sample (in 1D, 𝒪((Nt)4/3polylog(Nt/ε))) at sampling complexity Θ(ε−2). Achieves 𝒪(Ntpolylog(Nt/ε)) for sparsely dissipative lattice dynamics.

Grade 0.372 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Kaoru Mizuta

Figure

Schematic of patching and merging strategies for generic local Lindbladians: decomposition into blocks of size Rp with boundary regions of size R, followed by merging to absorb backward time evolution.

Asks

Can quantum simulation algorithms for generic lattice Lindbladians achieve gate counts approaching the fundamental lower bound Ω(Nt) while retaining polylogarithmic error scaling?

Before

Best previous gate count for generic lattice Lindbladian observables with polylogarithmic error scaling was 𝒪((Nt)3/2polylog(Nt/ε)) via extrapolation of second-order product formulas.

But

Finite-range interactions and dissipation on d-dimensional lattices with d∈𝒪(1). Generic algorithm estimates observables via sampling rather than outputting coherent quantum states.

Tools

dissipative patching lemma · reversed dynamics merging · quasi-probabilistic sampling · linear combination of unitaries

Abstract

Simulating the dynamics of dissipative quantum many-body systems governed by local Lindbladians is a fundamental task in quantum computation. While the near-optimal gate count has been achieved for Hamiltonian simulation, comparable results for Lindbladian simulation remain elusive. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for lattice Lindbladians by exploiting their locality. First, we consider sparsely dissipative systems, in which the dissipation is sparsely located, including boundary-driven systems. We establish a near-optimal quantum algorithm for their dynamics with gate count O(Nt polylog(Nt/ε)), where N is the system size, t is the evolution time, and ε is the allowable error. We then consider generic lattice Lindbladians with finite-range interactions and dissipation, and develop an algorithm for simulating time-evolved observables with gate count O((Nt)^(4/3) polylog(Nt/ε)) per sample with the sampling complexity Θ(ε⁻²). The gate count has the smallest known dependence on the system size among algorithms retaining polylogarithmic dependence on 1/ε. Our algorithms are based on two techniques that exploit locality: patching and merging. Patching decomposes dissipative dynamics into dynamics on subsystems with exponentially small error, generalizing a key idea underlying the Haah-Hastings-Kothari-Low algorithm for near-optimal Hamiltonian simulation. Merging absorbs reversed dissipative dynamics into other parts of the evolution, substantially reducing the overhead associated with quasi-probabilistic sampling. These results demonstrate that locality can be fully exploited to achieve fast quantum simulation of dissipative many-body dynamics, opening the way to applications such as predicting nonequilibrium phenomena and preparing desirable quantum states.

item.title: Real-Frequency Diagrammatics with Pole Representations
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Diagrammatic many-body perturbation theory is solved directly on real-frequency axis using systematically improvable complex pole and moment expansions. Controlled ESPRIT-based recompression truncates pole count, avoiding pole proliferation in self-consistent GW and second-order Born (GF2) calculations.

Grade 0.359 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Rayan Farid, Lei Zhang, Aiman Al-Eryani, Agnieszka Jażdżewska, Emanuel Gull

Figure

Pole counts for retarded self-energy, screened interaction, and spectral function versus compression tolerance ε (left) and iteration step (right) for GW on a half-filled Bethe lattice (U/t=2, βt=10). Recompression bounds the number of poles across self-consistency iterations.

Asks

Can real-frequency finite-temperature diagrammatics be evaluated self-consistently without grid discretization or numerical analytic continuation while controlling pole proliferation?

But

Equilibrium Keldysh framework, weak-coupling conserving approximations without vertex corrections.

Tools

Keldysh formalism · Prony-type approximation · ESPRIT signal processing · self-consistent GW and GF2 · Cauchy-Stieltjes transforms

Abstract

Finite-temperature many-body theories are typically formulated in imaginary time, where they are amenable to efficient numerical treatment. However, the extraction of spectral properties from the imaginary axis is difficult and requires numerical analytic continuation, while a direct formulation on the real axis requires prohibitively expensive numerical quadrature. In this paper, we represent the objects of many-body perturbation theory using systematically improvable pole and moment expansions and develop the corresponding framework for evaluating diagrammatic contributions directly on the real axis. We introduce a controlled recompression procedure that prevents the proliferation of poles under algebraic and diagrammatic operations. We benchmark the approach on paradigmatic quantum impurity problems and apply it to self-consistent calculations of the uniform electron gas. The resulting spectral quantities converge systematically towards numerical accuracy. This work provides a practical framework for controlled and systematically improvable calculations of spectral quantities within diagrammatic many-body theories, including self-consistent conserving approaches.
